label: Tutuila concrete and painted sheet roofs
character: Enclosed concrete and block houses with pale cream, warm white or subdued blue render; painted timber is a secondary finish. Galvanized, dark red and green sheet-metal roofs contrast with light walls. Flat concrete roofs remain visible urban alternatives; Manu’a does not inherit generic thatched resort roofs.
scope: 2015 household survey documents concrete walls and metal roofs across the territory. It does not measure paint frequency; colors translate the material categories into a restrained tropical palette. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: American Samoa 2015 HIES
evidence.note: Concrete walls and metal roofs dominate the surveyed dwelling inventory, including Manu’a; poured roof alternatives remain documented.

weight_basis.construction: 2015 HIES documents concrete walls throughout Tutuila and Manua; a rural location must not switch the territory to mostly wood. Metal covering dominates; poured roofs are secondary. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: The inspected completed FEMA house supports a pale neutral rendered wall and light corrugated roof with darker veranda wood. Census material stock remains authoritative for broader mix. The single recovery-program photograph does not establish current national paint frequencies; secondary colored sheets remain authored inference.

visual_references.scope: FEMA photograph of actual completed post-tsunami house, report Figure 9; one recovery program example from 2010.
visual_references.observed: Pale gray-cream rendered block walls, very light corrugated roof, dark brown veranda posts and fascia, low wide gable. Temporary tarps on neighboring work are excluded.

scope: Station infrastructure only. AANBUS sources document insulated panels and steel frames; expedition diaries identify red and green accommodation cladding. Existing simple forms are compatibility approximations for mapped footprints, not accurate reproductions of station engineering or all national programs. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

Contemporary render ranges from warm white to greige with charcoal roofing. Tropical timber/metal traditions and local sandstone remain separate regional choices.
scope: Newcastle heritage guidance anchors older eastern stock; the NSW pattern book supports contemporary blonde brick and white upper stories. These examples do not define one national style or override tropical and state-specific forms. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.scope: Pre-cyclone housing inventory, table 44 and cover photograph
evidence.note: Table 44 records 57,828 concrete, 33,515 timber-frame/wood and 50,352 timber-frame/tin-iron houses. The cover shows damaged ordinary coastal village stock; white emergency tents are excluded from finish interpretation.

Table 44 gives 50,352 tin-clad versus 33,515 wood-clad timber-frame houses; the explicit corrugated wall alternative therefore receives about three-fifths of the lightweight wall pool. Density-specific splits remain editorial approximations.
weight_basis.finishes: The government cover photograph supports pale sheet roofs, pale walls and a green sheet-roof alternative; repaired roofs and emergency tents prevent any reliable paint-frequency count. Corrugated wall versus wood weights use the housing inventory, while cream/green/blue paint weights remain conservative authored choices pending broader ordinary-stock photos.

weight_basis.finishes: An actual 2025 Jenrok family-home photograph supports a secondary salmon rendered wall with dark neutral trim. The close view gives no roof evidence; neutral sheet-roof dominance remains a stock-based authored approximation, not a photographed national color distribution.

visual_references.scope: Wilmer Joel original June 2025 photograph of a Jenrok family receiving their newly built house; close facade view only.
visual_references.observed: Salmon-pink textured render, dark purple-gray vertical trim, light window frames and metal security grille. Roof and entire facade distribution are outside the photograph.

label: Low masonry and painted lightweight walls beneath metal
character: Rendered concrete and lightweight painted wall panels use cream, pale gray-green and faded blue. Gray or off-white metal roofs are complemented by subdued red and green sheets; modern flat concrete roofs remain secondary. Natural palm thatch is not inferred for contemporary Nauruan housing.
scope: The 2021 census roof categories document an overwhelming metal-roof inventory and very few traditional roofs. Pigment alternatives are art choices within those manufactured material categories, not a measured color survey. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Nauru 2021 Census roof materials
evidence.note: The census roof variable identifies metal/iron/aluminium, concrete and wood; traditional roofing is scarcely represented.

evidence.title: Nauru 2021 census analytical report, housing materials
evidence.note: Figure 56 records 91.3% metal/iron/aluminium roofs, 5.8% concrete/cement/bricks and 1.1% asbestos; wall categories include 54.8% concrete/cement/bricks and 16.0% masonite.

weight_basis.construction: 2021 national report records 91.3% metal roofs and 5.8% concrete/cement/bricks. Wall materials include 54.8% concrete/cement/bricks and 16% masonite. The 70:24:6 envelope ranks retain a small slab component; painted fibre-panel housing is approximated by the lightweight envelope without asserting every such wall is timber.
weight_basis.finishes: The inspected six-house field sample supports pale cream/white walls, muted green-blue lower portions and a secondary matte gray corrugated roof finish. Its 2015 legacy-material targeting cannot establish current national prevalence; newer metal-roof census evidence retains leading neutral coated/metal sheets. Variant 2 represents the matte physical surface, with no chemistry inferred from color. The matte legacy finish has weight 2 among 100 sheet finishes, bounded by the much newer census rather than the targeted six-house photograph sample.

visual_references.scope: DFAT/SPREP 2015 field report, printed page 20, photos 5–10: six actual houses selected for legacy sheet-roof survey.
visual_references.observed: Pale cream/white wall panels or render, muted blue-green lower walls and posts, gray/brown matte corrugated roofs. This targeted legacy sample is not the contemporary national paint distribution.

label: Nouméa render, colonial boards and metal roofing
character: Contemporary pale rendered masonry coexists with painted timber or fibre-cement cladding. Cream, dusty ochre, soft sage and white walls support red, charcoal-green and gray sheet roofs. Kanak vegetal buildings remain locally significant but are not a substitute for Nouméa’s modern housing.
scope: ISEE’s dwelling questionnaire explicitly separates masonry, timber/cladding, sheet metal and vegetal/lime/earth walls and distinguishes Melanesian houses from ordinary houses and apartments. Roofing palette emphasizes locally documented sheet construction. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: ISEE 2025 dwelling questionnaire
evidence.note: Lists block/cement/brick, wood/cladding/fibre-cement, metal and vegetal/lime/earth wall classes.

evidence.title: ISEE construction materials bulletin
evidence.note: Tracks sheet-metal roofing and timber/metal framing as separate construction products.

evidence.title: SIC: sixty years of housing, 2016
evidence.note: Actual Tuband aerial and Païamboué2 completed timber housing; discussion distinguishes timber construction from masonry, and avoids equating all urban houses with concrete terraces.

weight_basis.construction: ISEE distinguishes masonry, wood/fibre-cement, sheet and vegetal construction; Noumea urban stock differs from tribal rural areas. Vegetal buildings remain a bounded rural option. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Inspected actual Tuband stock supports a substantial red/burgundy roof alternative with pale rendered walls; exact sheet versus ceramic profile cannot be determined from this aerial alone. The documented Koné timber homes support a smaller pale yellow-green painted-cladding option with pale sheet roof. These scoped 2016 photographs do not imply that all tribal settlements or contemporary Nouméa share one uniform distribution.

visual_references.scope: SIC 2016 publication: Tuband actual mixed housing aerial (page79) and completed Païamboué2 timber housing, Koné (page107). Upload date2025 is not construction date.
visual_references.observed: Tuband has many red/burgundy pitched roofs, pale rendered walls and white/gray flatter roofs; Koné timber example is pale yellow-green painted cladding, white frames, pale green sheet roof and darker veranda wood.

label: Light weatherboards, red or charcoal metal and masonry
character: Cream or white painted timber weatherboards, muted greige cladding and dark roof contrasts are essential. Brick and rendered modern homes share the catalog; timber is not uniformly brown. Red iron, gray metal and charcoal roofing sit above light joinery, with soft sage boards as a restrained variant.
scope: BRANZ villa documentation anchors weatherboard construction; a documented Wellington restoration provides greige boards, white joinery and a dark roof. Historic villas do not define all contemporary housing or regional stone stock. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: BRANZ Renovate: Villas
evidence.note: Documents rusticated and overlapping weatherboards and historic roof detailing.

evidence.title: Wellington villa color restoration
evidence.note: The paint supplier records pale greige weatherboards, white joinery and a dark roof for this project.

weight_basis.construction: BRANZ villa guidance supports painted horizontal weatherboards and iron roofing; modern brick/render alternatives remain. This is an editorial national fallback, not a historic-villa-only census. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Inspected Wellington villa directly establishes painted horizontal boards, white joinery and corrugated sheet profile. Source explicitly names a dark roof paint, so cool photographic reflection is not sampled as pale metal pigment. Red/green iron and brick/render alternatives rely on cited broader villa/stock guidance; relative weights are editorial.

visual_references.scope: Hannah Kang Wellington villa exterior photographed for paint supplier; specifically restored villa stock, not all New Zealand.
visual_references.observed: Horizontal pale gray weatherboards, white joinery, red entrance door and corrugated roof; roof appears lighter in cool illumination but source names dark Nocturnal paint. Neighboring pale weatherboard home is also visible.

regions.label: Tokelau light corrugated roofs over concrete and timber
regions.scope: Tokelau is grouped under New Zealand in the source administrative atlas but has its own atoll building stock. The2016 HIES metadata is a sample-case inventory, not a population census; avoid mainland suburban palette inheritance.

evidence.title: Tokelau2016 HIES metadata
evidence.scope: Roof and wall sample variables, PDF pages49–51
evidence.note: 119 sampled main houses:106 corrugated roofs and13 concrete roofs; roof-color responses41 white,71 light,4 medium,3 unpainted and0 dark/rusted. Wall cases82 concrete,32 wood,3 corrugated,2 traditional. Metadata warns case frequencies are not population statistics.

evidence.title: Government of Tokelau Asset Management Plan2015–30
evidence.note: Confirms corrugated roofing prevalence and marine exposure; describes concrete buildings and timber weatherboard residences.

weight_basis.construction: Concrete/render leads, timber remains substantial, and slab roofs remain a small alternative. This is an authored approximation informed by HIES case ordering and the asset inventory; published case percentages are not asserted as population shares.
weight_basis.finishes: Roof whiteness/lightness has direct survey evidence: use white and light gray corrugated finishes, with a small medium-gray option. Exact hues remain authored approximations. Wall paint is conservatively pale pending ordinary-stock photographs; no mainland brick, terracotta tiles or dominant charcoal roof mix.

label: Concrete hurricane houses and later painted timber
character: Older hurricane houses have pale concrete walls, frequently under replacement iron roofs; later modern housing includes timber and concrete. White, cream and restrained sage boarding pair with gray, dark green and oxide-red sheet roofing. Coral-limestone buildings are a documented minority.
scope: The national 2017 household report distinguishes hurricane and modern housing and replacement of fibrolite by iron after Cyclone Heta. Colors are restrained authoring choices; the limestone tourist example establishes material presence, not prevalence. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Niue Household and Population Census 2017
evidence.note: Housing chapter describes concrete hurricane houses and later timber/concrete modern dwellings, with widespread iron roof replacement.

evidence.title: Niue Tourism accommodation inventory
evidence.note: Stone Villa’s is explicitly described as limestone construction.

weight_basis.construction: 2019 census describes concrete hurricane houses and later wood/concrete houses, with widespread replacement iron roofs. Rural Niue therefore remains substantially concrete, not majority timber or thatch. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Two former family homes visibly pair white walls with very pale corrugated roofs; these lead authored weights. One Hakupu limestone house supports a bounded rubble-stone option, not a national prevalence estimate. Its dusk lighting is excluded from pigment selection. Red and green roofs remain secondary stock-based inferences requiring wider daytime sampling.

visual_references.scope: Refurbished Alofi family home photographed by official Niue Tourism.
visual_references.observed: Pale white/gray walls, white corrugated roof, dark veranda and window trim. Wall substrate cannot be identified from this photograph alone.

visual_references.scope: Former family home now a guesthouse; ordinary low domestic envelope.
visual_references.observed: White painted upper wall panels and lower masonry, white fascia and frames, pale gray corrugated gable roof.

visual_references.scope: Bounded limestone house at Hakupu, photographed at dusk.
visual_references.observed: Uncoursed exposed limestone walls under a dark shallow sheet roof. Warm lamps preclude deriving daytime stone RGB.

label: Pale cottages, pine boards and Kingston stone
character: Contemporary timber or sheet-clad cottages use cream, white and restrained pale green; gray or green metal roofs accompany them. Kingston retains pale stone/render and pine joinery, with hand-split timber shingles on bounded heritage buildings. Dark basalt masonry does not replace the light domestic palette.
scope: Local historical accounts document timber/fibro town buildings and pine/shingle heritage details. Heritage shingle roofing is one bounded alternative, not a claim that all modern Burnt Pine homes have wooden roofs. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Holloway’s Store and Burnt Pine
evidence.note: Documents timber and fibro construction with verandahs in the town center.

evidence.title: The Settlement Guardhouse
evidence.note: Records restoration using hand-split Norfolk Pine roof shingles.

evidence.title: Norfolk Government House
evidence.note: Documents Norfolk Island Pine joinery and bounded Regency heritage color restoration.

weight_basis.construction: Holloways Store documents timber/fibro town construction; Kingston stone and pine-shingle restoration is a bounded heritage context, not a quarter of every rural settlement. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Ferny Lane provides a bounded contemporary example of pale horizontal and vertical painted boarding with dark sheet roof/posts. Its twilight blue cast is excluded from literal RGB matching. Light siding leads, darker sheet roofs remain secondary; the heritage timber-shingle option stays small. Paint weights are authored, not a count of national dwellings.

visual_references.scope: Actual four-bedroom house near Burnt Pine, current tourism listing; twilight photo is unsuitable for measuring paint RGB.
visual_references.observed: Light gray-white horizontal weatherboards, vertical pale gable boarding, dark gray-blue metal roof and veranda posts. Roof blue cast cannot be separated from twilight sky color.

label: Concrete terraces and low metal-roofed masonry
character: Pale white, beige and muted coral render cover concrete and block walls. Flat concrete roofs are prominent; pitched metal alternatives use silver, light gray, red-brown or gray-green sheets. Lightweight timber remains a secondary stock rather than a tropical resort stereotype.
scope: CNMI Commerce inventories explicitly document concrete/block walls and both concrete and metal roofs. Saipan/Tinian/Rota differences remain; choices are not estimated roof shares. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: CNMI HIES 2016 housing
evidence.note: Housing inventory reports predominantly poured concrete or concrete-block walls.

evidence.title: CNMI 2017 roof material inventory
evidence.note: Occupied dwellings are split between concrete roofs and metal roofs, with other materials a small minority.

weight_basis.construction: Commerce housing tables identify predominantly concrete/block walls and both concrete and metal roofs. Town/rural mixtures preserve masonry and allow more pitched metal without replacing the stock with timber. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Actual2018 Koblerville damaged home: unfinished gray concrete blocks, timber roof framing and displaced pale corrugated metal. Roof removed by cyclone, so no original roof pitch is inferred. Interior-facing block may have been rendered externally; add only a bounded unfinished-block candidate, not universal bare masonry. Brick bond map approximates concrete-block coursing; no new material texture required. Neutral painted/rendered census-based stock remains leading.

visual_references.scope: USAF TechSgt JoshuaGarcia roof-assessment field photograph, November2018, Saipan. Damaged stock selection, not random prevalence survey.
visual_references.observed: Actual2018 Koblerville damaged home: unfinished gray concrete blocks, timber roof framing and displaced pale corrugated metal. Roof removed by cyclone, so no original roof pitch is inferred. Interior-facing block may have been rendered externally; add only a bounded unfinished-block candidate, not universal bare masonry.

label: Koror concrete and timber with sheet-metal roofs
character: Light concrete/block or painted timber houses sit under silver, red-brown and green sheet roofs; urban concrete terraces accompany the pitched stock. Warm white, pale mint and light sand contrast with dark green joinery. Ceremonial bai ornament and thatch are excluded from ordinary household defaults.
scope: The government yearbook tabulates wall and roof construction by state and year. Material roles are evidence-based; this restrained color ensemble is illustrative and does not imply ceremonial buildings are generic houses. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Palau 2020 Statistical Yearbook
evidence.note: Housing tables separately enumerate wall and roof materials across states, including concrete, wood and metal.

weight_basis.construction: 2020 statistical yearbook distinguishes concrete/wood and manufactured roofing across states. The ceremonial bai is not a substitute for ordinary household stock. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Actual Ngiwal local-house photographs support green horizontal painted boards, pale corrugated roof and dark wood joinery. The 2003 Koror street supports pale masonry low-rise stock but is historical. Green remains a secondary authored alternative; ceremonial bai painting is not copied onto ordinary homes and these samples do not establish current national frequencies.

visual_references.scope: Matsumoto Kazuto original Ngiwal local-house photographs, with 2003 Koror street context inspected separately.
visual_references.observed: Vivid green horizontal painted boards and green fascia, pale corrugated gable roof, brown timber doors and an adjacent gray sheet-clad outbuilding. Koror street includes pale rendered dwellings with shallow light roofs.

label: Timber and palm villages with metal-roofed urban masonry
character: Rural timber, palm and woven-wall traditions retain warm fiber and wood tones; imported gray metal roofs coexist with brown thatch. Modern centers add painted cream, pale green or blue cladding and light rendered masonry. No single highland or coastal house type stands for the whole country.
scope: The 2023 rural household survey covers selected study areas and distinguishes thatched and corrugated-metal roofing, including more permanent materials near Kokopo. These are bounded rural observations, not national housing shares; urban modern forms remain explicit. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: PNG 2023 Rural Household Survey
evidence.note: Household building-material section records thatch and corrugated roofs, palm and timber flooring, and differences among surveyed regions.

weight_basis.construction: 2024 household survey documents large rural thatch/palm/timber differences from contemporary town materials. Natural wall/roof vocabulary remains substantial outside cities; no single coastal or highland archetype stands for all provinces. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Scoped actual photographs constrain material and pigment presence; authored relative weights remain prevalence approximations, not a national color survey. Viewed brown vertical organic/wood wall strips with exposed framing and weathered brown thatch. Painted horizontal weatherboard must not substitute for these unpainted rural walls. No claim that an individual village covers all PNG house traditions.

visual_references.scope: Anthropologist Joel Robbins original Urapmin village photograph; highland rural stock, not urban PNG.
visual_references.observed: Viewed brown vertical organic/wood wall strips with exposed framing and weathered brown thatch. Painted horizontal weatherboard must not substitute for these unpainted rural walls. No claim that an individual village covers all PNG house traditions.

label: Adamstown timber and corrugated rainwater roofs
character: Small timber houses and modern mixed timber/concrete buildings use natural weathered brown, cream and subdued green painted boards. Gray, dark gray, oxide red and green metal roofs collect rainwater. The domestic catalog applies to Adamstown, not the uninhabited Henderson, Ducie or Oeno islands.
scope: The government’s historical administrative report documents local timber and replacement of thatch by corrugated iron. Current official homestays show continuing wooden dwelling types; these are bounded examples, not a comprehensive modern census. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Pitcairn administrative report by J. S. Neill
evidence.note: Historical official report records unpainted local timber houses and corrugated iron roofs collecting water.

evidence.title: Pitcairn official homestays
evidence.note: Lists existing home accommodation including the Pitcairn Log House.

weight_basis.construction: Adamstown is the sole settlement; historical local-timber/rain-catching iron roofs and current home accommodation support a timber-led mixture. Identical settlement-class weights reflect one actual tiny stock, not invented towns on Henderson/Oeno/Ducie. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: The directly inspected resident Log House exterior establishes green horizontal cladding beneath pale corrugated metal. Older local-timber descriptions justify a smaller natural-wood alternative; cream boards are a conservative stock inference. Roof red/green alternatives were removed without clear inspected exterior support.

visual_references.scope: Local resident Tania Christian home in Adamstown shown by Pitcairn Islands Tourism; exterior log+house11 image.
visual_references.observed: Low house with dark green horizontal cladding, pale corrugated iron roof, green porch posts and red-brown porch deck. Despite its name, visible walls are painted green rather than uniformly raw brown timber.

label: Pale Apia masonry and open-fale timber traditions
character: Apia’s cement and timber houses use cream, white and restrained pale blue or green finishes beneath mostly iron roofs. Rural fale construction retains natural timber and a bounded palm-thatch alternative. Silver, deep red and green manufactured roofing remain visible across enclosed modern houses.
scope: Samoa’s housing census distinguishes more cement/wood enclosure in Apia and numerous open-wall fales in rural regions. Closed forms cannot recreate open ceremonial or living fales, and the traditional roof alternative is not a claim of modern prevalence. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Samoa 2016 Census housing brief
evidence.note: Documents iron roofs and regional distinction between cement/wood enclosure and rural open-wall fales.

weight_basis.construction: 2016 census distinguishes enclosed and open buildings and records 71% European-style footprints. Open fale is not synonymous with thatch: iron roofs cover both types. Geometry cannot fully represent open-sided fale; metal remains predominant. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: The inspected family-built room supports a bounded exposed gray-block wall alternative and leading pale corrugated roof. Brick relief is used as an approximate modular concrete-block bond, with gray pigment; it does not assert fired red brick. Other painted walls remain authored conservative alternatives. One welfare project is not national prevalence evidence.

visual_references.scope: Charity original November2025 photograph of a family-built room beside a daughter’s fale near Apia, not a tourism reconstruction.
visual_references.observed: Unpainted gray concrete blocks, light corrugated metal roof, white door, blue-painted adjoining service-room wall. Purple curtains are excluded as window-frame paint.

label: Timber boards and bush materials beyond Honiara masonry
character: Timber is essential in both town and rural walls; natural medium browns, cream paint and faded green boards are paired with gray or red metal sheets. Traditional bush walls and brown thatch remain substantial outside towns. Modern rendered concrete is included without turning Honiara into uniformly masonry stock.
scope: The 2019 census tables support timber-heavy walls even in Honiara; nearby narrative text reverses denominators, so the actual wall table guides these choices. Traditional rural construction is reduced to existing surfaces without adding geometry. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Solomon Islands 2019 Census
evidence.note: Wall-material tables show extensive timber and traditional material use, while masonry is a smaller category; regional tables distinguish Honiara.

weight_basis.construction: 2019 national census records extensive timber and traditional walls, with more manufactured materials in Honiara. Rural bush materials remain distinct from painted town boards. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Actual Angouru village supports pale corrugated roofing, brown thatch, unpainted light-tan woven walls and a small corrugated wall component. Explicit woven-panel variant 2 approximates the visible crossed organic ribbons; weave scale is illustrative, not species-measured. This rural Malaita sample supports those alternatives without defining Honiara or nationwide paint frequencies.

visual_references.scope: UNDP 2025 aerial photograph of actual Angouru village, South Malaita.
visual_references.observed: Pale corrugated metal roofs with occasional rusted/replacement sheets, brown thatch roofs, light tan woven wall panels and gray corrugated wall sheeting. Solar panels remain equipment, not roof pigment.

label: Research quarters and painted whaling-station remnants
character: King Edward Point has pale occupied buildings with red roofs and bounded green service buildings. The finishes apply only to the documented station and heritage footprint inventory; no residential settlement is inferred elsewhere on South Georgia or the South Sandwich Islands.
scope: King Edward Point research/administration and bounded historical sites. BAS documents building histories and current facilities; mandatory domestic-form slots approximate mapped small structures only. Precise historic paint schemes require named-site overrides. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: BAS station and refuge building history
evidence.note: Documents King Edward Point administrative and research buildings, surviving and removed structures.

evidence.title: BAS King Edward Point facility
evidence.note: Documents the current research station and its limited operational purpose.

weight_basis.construction: There is no ordinary residential stock. The cited territorial or research authority bounds existing mapped operational/heritage structures. All settlement classes use one inert low-envelope compatibility form; the palette does not create buildings or settlements. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Directly inspected King Edward Point field photograph and BAS station records agree on pale occupied buildings with red roofs plus green service sheds. The5:1 red/green roof ranks describe this small operational cluster, not an Antarctic residential survey.

visual_references.scope: Original field photograph DSC_0090 of King Edward Point from across the bay; BAS independently identifies the station context.
visual_references.observed: Long pale-white occupied buildings have dark red pitched roofs; green-gray roofed service sheds and pale window/door surrounds remain secondary. Early/late light warms white walls but does not make them brown timber.

label: Painted wood and cement homes under iron
character: Light cement walls and cream, white or soft-green timber boards sit below metal roofing in gray, dark red and green. Pale modern render and small concrete terraces coexist with pitched homes; thatched fale are a documented minority and are not the ordinary roof palette.
scope: Tonga census roof categories establish extensive metal use and small traditional-roof counts. The contemporary 2021 dictionary confirms separate roof and wall material fields; paint colors are authored, not census measurements. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Tonga 2011 Census roof materials
evidence.note: Roof inventory distinguishes metal, concrete, wood and thatch, with metal by far the largest category.

evidence.title: Tonga 2021 housing dictionary
evidence.note: Maintains separate dwelling-type, wall-material and roof-material variables.

weight_basis.construction: Census roof inventory strongly favors metal; reconstructed and older cement/timber homes coexist. Traditional fale roofing is not promoted to equal share of ordinary residential covering. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Inspected Tongatapu house supports leading white horizontal boarding, a blue joinery alternative and neutral corrugated roof. Patchy oxidation is not relabeled red paint. Census establishes the broader metal/concrete/wood mix; colored alternatives have authored weights rather than a national photographic frequency estimate.

visual_references.scope: Architectural field photograph of ordinary Tongatapu house, distinct from ceremonial fale photographs.
visual_references.observed: White horizontal weatherboards, blue window and lower-wall trim, gray corrugated roof with patchy oxide rust, neighboring pale sheet roof. Rust patches do not imply a uniformly red-painted roof.

label: Funafuti light masonry and outer-island timber with iron roofs
character: Light concrete/block and painted timber dwellings use warm white, pale mint and soft blue beneath rain-catching corrugated iron. Silver and light gray dominate the visual choices, with muted green and red metal alternatives. Traditional outer-island structures are locally bounded; a universal thatch treatment would misrepresent Funafuti.
scope: Tuvalu’s electricity master plan explicitly describes widespread Funafuti corrugated iron roofing. The census inventory includes construction, roof and floor materials; no national paint frequency is claimed. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Tuvalu renewable electricity master plan
evidence.note: Government plan hosted by UN ESCAP describes Funafuti roofs as predominantly corrugated iron.

evidence.title: Tuvalu 2017 housing census
evidence.note: Housing coverage includes living-quarter construction and roof-material variables.

weight_basis.construction: Government energy planning describes Funafuti corrugated roofs; household census distinguishes walls and roofs. Outer-island traditional construction is bounded without overriding the populated atoll baseline. Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Inspected Funafuti photographs support neutral corrugated roof/wall sheets and a smaller bare brown timber component. The sample is historical and deliberately records poor sanitation; it cannot establish present national paint frequencies. Neutral light walls/roofs remain leading authored choices; blue tarps and laundry do not become permanent paint alternatives.

visual_references.scope: David Wilson original April 2010 photographs of Funafuti borrow-pit houses; historical low-income settlement, not all national stock or current condition.
visual_references.observed: Gray-white corrugated roofs and wall sheets, brown timber panels, concrete block bases and muted green wall patches. Bright blue tarps and hanging laundry are excluded as building paint evidence.

label: Sparse refuge and airfield infrastructure
character: Mapped Midway historic officers quarters are pale two-storey buildings with low nearly flat gray roofs and dark window openings. Other refuge and airfield structures require site-specific finishes; this scattered island group has no domestic national vernacular.
scope: Infrastructure only; Midway is the documented example and does not define the other scattered islands. FWS describes staff/volunteer facilities and surviving historic resources; NPS documents military-era construction. Mandatory forms are compatibility approximations for source footprints. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: FWS Midway Atoll
evidence.note: Documents refuge staff accommodation, infrastructure and protected historical resources.

evidence.title: NPS Midway historic facilities
evidence.note: Documents the bounded military and later service building inventory.

weight_basis.finishes: Inspected USFWS photograph supports a single pale facade/dark gray low-roof pairing for the documented officers quarters. Quiet plaster is a shader approximation for an unresolved smooth/panel substrate; pitched matte sheet remains an inert compatibility option, not a photographed roof claim.

visual_references.scope: USFWS field image by Jon Brack,2023 Seabird Protection Project, three historical officers houses on Midway.
visual_references.observed: Repeated white two-storey house facades, nearly flat gray roofs, dark window openings and front verandas. The image does not establish exposed roof chemistry or facade substrate; quiet pale surfaces are an explicit visual approximation.

label: Port Vila masonry and rural wood/bush walls
character: Modern towns combine pale rendered concrete and painted timber with silver or muted red metal roofs. Rural islands retain warm timber/bush surfaces and brown traditional roofing. Soft ochre, cream and gray-green pigments separate contemporary walls from raw wood; neither urban concrete nor thatched bungalows represent the whole archipelago.
scope: The 2020 national analytical report explicitly separates roof and wall materials by urban/rural residence and province. Traditional roofs are reserved as one rural-capable alternative; modern stock remains present in all density bands. RGB values are authored sRGB approximations, not measured census paint colors.

evidence.title: Vanuatu 2020 Census Analytical Report
evidence.note: Construction tables and figures distinguish urban metal roofs from the considerable rural traditional-roof stock.

evidence.title: Vanuatu Homes building specifications
evidence.note: A local builder specifies corrugated coated-steel roofs for its contemporary houses.

Relative weights are authored prevalence ranks, not measured percentages or a census-to-geometry equivalence.
weight_basis.finishes: Actual VSO fieldworkers November2011 Butmas village overview: several low enclosed tan/brown organic-panel houses under brown weathered palm-thatch gables. Church/classroom interiors and tourist bungalows are excluded from ordinary-house pigment inference. Traditional wall panel is represented by woven TIMBER_WALL variant2 with restrained tan; coexisting raw strips retain variant0. Census-supported modern town construction remains explicit. Weights are authored broad ranks, not measured village or national paint shares.

visual_references.scope: Original Annie/Rupert fieldwork photo, Butmas highland village, central Santo; scoped rural reference, not national prevalence.
visual_references.observed: Actual VSO fieldworkers November2011 Butmas village overview: several low enclosed tan/brown organic-panel houses under brown weathered palm-thatch gables. Church/classroom interiors and tourist bungalows are excluded from ordinary-house pigment inference. Traditional wall panel is represented by woven TIMBER_WALL variant2 with restrained tan; coexisting raw strips retain variant0. Census-supported modern town construction remains explicit.

label: Masonry and local timber beneath tôle roofs
character: Pale cement/block homes and cream or soft-blue timber cladding are capped by gray, white, green or red sheet-metal roofs. Traditional fale remain more relevant on Futuna than Wallis, while contemporary manufactured materials remain central. Dark volcanic stone belongs to explicit masonry examples, not every house.
scope: IEOM documents block walls and sheet roofs, with a stronger historic fale presence on Futuna. The dated inventory anchors material vocabulary, not current percentages; later builder testimony supports continued local timber construction.
